mcqs.question: Two frequently-used blocks map to the same slot in a direct-mapped cache and keep evicting each other, even though most of the cache is idle. What is this called?
mcqs.explanation: This is the textbook conflict miss: a miss that wouldn't occur in a fully associative cache of the same size, caused purely by both blocks being forced into the same single slot. Capacity misses are about total working-set size, compulsory misses are first-touch, and coherence misses are a multiprocessor phenomenon.

mcqs.question: Why do nearly all real L1/L2/L3 caches use set-associative placement instead of direct-mapped or fully associative?
options: It's the only scheme that supports write-back caching
It captures most of fully associative's conflict-avoidance benefit while needing only N comparators per set instead of one per entire cache
It's required by the cache coherence protocol
It uses less silicon area than direct-mapped caches
mcqs.explanation: Set-associative is the practical middle ground: it needs far less comparison hardware than fully associative (N comparators per set, not one per slot in the whole cache) while avoiding most of direct-mapped's conflict misses. Write-back and coherence are independent of placement policy, and it typically uses more area than direct-mapped, not less.

mcqs.question: A cache is reorganized from direct-mapped (64 sets) to 4-way set-associative at the same total capacity (so 16 sets of 4 ways). What happens to the index and tag field widths?
options: Index grows by 2 bits, tag shrinks by 2 bits
Index shrinks by 2 bits, tag grows by 2 bits
Both stay exactly the same size
Offset shrinks to make room for extra tag bits
mcqs.explanation: Fewer sets (64 -> 16 is a 4x reduction) means fewer index bits are needed to select among them (2 fewer bits), and those bits shift into the tag field instead. The offset field, which only depends on line size, is unaffected by associativity.
